This page is the interactive version of the lesson notes (PDF). Each section
starts with a problem in a game. Then it explains the idea behind it. It ends
with a **Do it** task and one set of questions. The full explanations,
examples and exercises are in the notes.

## Key terms

{{< glossary game-loop frame-rate coordinate-system origin axis coordinate ordered-pair quadrant screen-space world-space tile-grid handedness >}}

## 1.1 Mathematics in game development

- For a computer, a game is numbers in memory: positions, health, score.
- The **game loop** repeats: read the input → update the numbers → draw.
- One pass makes one **frame**.
- **Frame time** = 1000 / **frame rate** milliseconds. At 60 fps: about 16.7 ms.
- All the work of a frame must fit into the frame time.
- Coordinates and vectors (weeks 1–3), trigonometry (4), matrices (5–7),
  logic (9–10), probability (11–13).

![The game loop.](images/game-loop.png){width=70%}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the mathematics in a game"}
Play a game on your phone for two minutes. Write four things it must compute
with numbers (for example "the position of my car"). Next to each, write the
mathematics it needs.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · The frame budget"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="16.7 ms|probability|draw the frame first"}
A game runs at 50 fps. Frame time?
:   20 ms

A game runs at 60 fps for 10 seconds. How many frames?
:   600

A game runs at 30 fps. Frame time?
:   about 33 ms

The game loop has read the input. What does it do next?
:   update the numbers

A turret must aim at a ship. Which mathematics does it need?
:   trigonometry
:::
:::

## 1.2 One-dimensional coordinates

- A **number line** has an **origin** (0), a unit and a positive direction.
- A point has one number: its **coordinate**.
- **Discrete**: only whole numbers (squares of a board game).
  **Continuous**: any number (a character at 3.27).
- **Displacement** = end − start. The sign shows the direction.
- **Distance** = the displacement without the sign. Never negative.

![A runner game: the player goes back from x = 4 to the checkpoint at x = −3.](images/number-line.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
A distance is never negative. −7 is a displacement; its distance is 7.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A runner track on paper"}
Draw a number line from −5 to 10. Mark a coin at 6, a trap at −2 and the start
at 0. The player runs from the start to the coin, then falls back to the
trap. Write the displacement and the distance of each move.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · Moving along a line"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="−8|0"}
The player goes from 4 back to the checkpoint at −3. Displacement?
:   −7

The distance of that move.
:   7

A platform moves from −2 to 6. Displacement?
:   8

A board game piece can only be on square 1, 2 or 3. What kind of positions?
:   discrete

A character can stand at x = 3.27. What kind of positions?
:   continuous
:::
:::

## 1.3 The two-dimensional coordinate system

- Two axes cross at the origin: the **x-axis** (right) and the **y-axis** (up).
- A point is an **ordered pair** (x, y). The order matters.
- Four **quadrants**: I (+, +), II (−, +), III (−, −), IV (+, −).
- A point with a 0 is on an axis, not in a quadrant.
- Designers often put the origin at the centre of a level. Then negative
  numbers are normal.

![The four quadrants and their signs.](images/quadrants.png){width=62%}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Build the level in GeoGebra"}
Open geogebra.org/calculator (free, no account). Type the points
`Coin = (4, 3)`, `Key = (-3, 2)`, `Trap = (-4, -2.5)`, `Exit = (2, -3)`. Check
their quadrants. Add an enemy in quadrant IV and a door on the y-axis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · Where is the point?"}
Choose the right answer. You can use an answer more than once.

::: {.match extra="quadrant I|on the y-axis"}
The key at (−3, 2).
:   quadrant II

The trap at (−4, −2.5).
:   quadrant III

A tree at (5, 0).
:   on the x-axis

The exit at (2, −3).
:   quadrant IV

From the key (−3, 2) to the coin (4, 3): how far to the right?
:   7 units
:::
:::

## 1.4 Screen space and world space

- **World space**: world units, y grows **up**, origin chosen by the designer.
- **Screen space**: pixels, origin at the **top left**, y grows **down**.
- Screen W × H pixels, centre (W/2, H/2), scale s pixels per unit:
  x~s~ = W/2 + s · x~w~ and y~s~ = H/2 − s · y~w~.
- From a touch back to the world: x~w~ = (x~s~ − W/2) / s and
  y~w~ = (H/2 − y~s~) / s.
- Example: W = 1080, H = 1920, s = 100. World (2, 3) → pixel (740, 660).

![The same point in world space and in screen space (s = 100).](images/screen-world.png){width=92%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
Screen y grows **down**. With a plus instead of the minus, the world is drawn
upside down.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/grid-strike.html" poster="sims/grid-strike.png" title="Grid Strike: hit the coordinates" kind="game" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Grid Strike"}
Play both stages of **Grid Strike**. Stage 2 uses screen coordinates. Write
your two scores and one point you missed. Why is stage 2 harder at first?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Convert between the spaces"}
A phone: W = 1080, H = 1920, scale s = 100. The world origin is in the centre.
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(740, 1260)|(2, −2)"}
The pixel at the centre of the screen.
:   (540, 960)

The pixel of the world point (2, 3).
:   (740, 660)

The pixel of the world point (−1, 2).
:   (440, 760)

The player touches pixel (340, 1160). Which world point?
:   (−2, −2)

The player touches pixel (840, 760). Which world point?
:   (3, 2)
:::
:::

## 1.5 Grids and tile maps

- On a grid, a position is a **column** c and a **row** r, counted from 0.
- Memory is one long list, so the grid is stored row after row.
- Index on a grid with n columns: i = r × n + c.
- Back: i ÷ n gives the row; the remainder is the column.
- One row up or down changes the index by n.

![An 8-column board: each cell has (c, r) and an index i.](images/tile-index.png){width=80%}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A board in a spreadsheet"}
In Excel or Google Sheets, make a board of 5 columns and 4 rows. Type the
index of each cell, row after row (0 to 19). Choose three cells and check
i = r × 5 + c.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · Boards and inventories"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="37|column 5, row 2"}
A board with 8 columns: the gem in column 5, row 3. Index?
:   29

The same board: in which column and row is index 42?
:   column 2, row 5

The same board: the index one row above index 42.
:   50

An inventory with 6 columns: column 4, row 2. Index?
:   16

The same inventory: where is index 23?
:   column 5, row 3
:::
:::

## 1.6 The three-dimensional coordinate system

- A third axis, **z**, at a right angle to x and y.
- A point is an **ordered triple** (x, y, z).
- If y points up, y is the height, and y = 0 is the ground.
- Hand rule: thumb +x, index finger +y, middle finger +z. Left hand: a
  **left-handed** system. Right hand: **right-handed**.
- Unity: y up, left-handed. Blender: z up, right-handed.
- Blender → Unity: swap the last two numbers, (x, y, z) → (x, z, y).

![Left-handed and right-handed coordinate systems.](images/handedness.png){width=86%}

{{< sim file="sims/position-3d.html" poster="images/axes-3d.png" title="Place an object in 3D" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Move a player in 3D"}
In the 3D viewer, move the player to (1, 2, 4). Which slider changes the
height? Then catch three coins and write their coordinates.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 6 · Positions in 3D"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="right-handed|(1, 4, 2)|x = 0"}
A drone at (4, 12, −3) in a y-up world. How high is it?
:   12 units

A lamp at (1, 4, 2) in Blender. Where is it in Unity?
:   (1, 2, 4)

A model at (2, −5, 3) in Blender. Where is it in Unity?
:   (2, 3, −5)

In a y-up world, all points on the ground have…
:   y = 0

The handedness of Unity.
:   left-handed
:::
:::

## Game challenge: Harbor Guard {.challenge}

Work alone. Use every section of today.

![A screen of Harbor Guard: the player taps a tile of the harbour grid.](images/harbor-guard.png){width=42%}

**Harbor Guard** is a tower-defence game for phones in portrait (1080 × 1920
pixels). The harbour is a grid of 9 columns of tiles, each 1 unit wide. The
camera shows the world origin in the centre of the screen, with a scale of
120 pixels per unit. The player taps a tile to build a tower. The game runs at
60 fps, and its 3D towers are made in Blender.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 7 · Taps and tiles (harder)"}
Use the numbers of Harbor Guard. Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(2, −1)|quadrant II|(3, 0, 5)"}
The frame time of the game.
:   about 16.7 ms

The player taps pixel (780, 840). Which world point?
:   (2, 1)

In which quadrant is that point?
:   quadrant I

The player taps pixel (420, 1080). Which world point?
:   (−1, −1)

The tile in column 4, row 2 of the harbour grid. Index?
:   22

A tower at (3, 0, 5) in Blender. Where is it in Unity?
:   (3, 5, 0)
:::
:::

## Summary {.summary}

- The game loop makes one frame per pass; frame time = 1000 / fps ms.
- Displacement = end − start; distance has no sign.
- (x, y): four quadrants, decided by the signs.
- Screen y grows down: world ↔ screen needs the centre, the scale and a minus sign.
- Grid index i = r × n + c.
- (x, y, z): Unity is y-up and left-handed, Blender z-up and right-handed.
